## Proof

**Setup.** Since $\sigma \circ \varphi = \mathrm{id}_R$, every $s \in S$ decomposes as $s = \varphi(\sigma(s)) + (s - \varphi(\sigma(s)))$ with $s - \varphi(\sigma(s)) \in I$. Thus $S = \varphi(R) \oplus I$ as $R$-modules, and $\sigma$ induces an isomorphism $S/I \xrightarrow{\sim} R$ with inverse $\varphi$. We identify $S/I = R$ throughout.

Since $I/I^2$ is a free $R$-module (of rank $d$, say), choose $t_1, \dots, t_d \in I$ whose images $\bar{t}_1, \dots, \bar{t}_d$ form an $R$-basis of $I/I^2$.

**Conormal sequence.** For the sequence of maps $R \xrightarrow{\varphi} S \to S/I = R$, the conormal exact sequence reads
$$I/I^2 \longrightarrow \Omega_{S/R} \otimes_S R \longrightarrow \Omega_{R/R} \longrightarrow 0.$$
Since $\Omega_{R/R} = 0$ (the map $R \to S/I = R$ is the identity), we get a surjection $I/I^2 \twoheadrightarrow \Omega_{S/R} \otimes_S R$. Because $\varphi$ is **smooth**, this sequence is also left-exact (a standard property of smooth maps: the conormal sequence $0 \to I/I^2 \to \Omega_{S/R}\otimes S/I \to \Omega_{(S/I)/R} \to 0$ is short exact). Hence
$$I/I^2 \cong \Omega_{S/R} \otimes_S R.$$
In particular, $dt_1, \dots, dt_d$ form a basis of $\Omega_{S/R} \otimes_S R$.

**Key consequence for derivations.** For any $R$-module $M$ (viewed as an $S$-module via $S \to S/I = R$), $R$-derivations $\delta: S \to M$ correspond to $S$-linear maps $\Omega_{S/R} \to M$, which (since $I$ acts trivially on $M$) correspond to $R$-linear maps $\Omega_{S/R} \otimes_S R \to M$, i.e., to $R$-linear maps $I/I^2 \to M$. Since $I/I^2$ is free on $\bar{t}_1, \dots, \bar{t}_d$, a derivation $\delta$ is uniquely determined by — and can be freely prescribed on — the values $\delta(t_1), \dots, \delta(t_d) \in M$.

---

**Constructing the map $\alpha: R[t_1,\dots,t_d] \to S$.** Define the $R$-algebra map $\alpha$ by $r \mapsto \varphi(r)$, $t_i \mapsto t_i$. Let $J = (t_1, \dots, t_d) \subset R[t_1, \dots, t_d]$. Since $\alpha(J) \subset I$, for each $n \geq 1$ we get an induced map
$$\alpha_n: R[t_1,\dots,t_d]/J^n \longrightarrow S/I^n.$$

**Constructing the inverse via formal smoothness.** Since $\varphi$ is smooth, $S$ is formally smooth over $R$. We build compatible $R$-algebra maps $\beta_n: S \to R[t_1,\dots,t_d]/J^n$ by induction on $n$, satisfying:

- (a) $\beta_n$ lifts $\beta_{n-1}$ (with $\beta_1 = \sigma: S \to R = R[t]/J$),
- (b) $\beta_n(t_i) \equiv t_i \pmod{J^n}$ for all $i$.

*Base case $n=1$:* $\beta_1 = \sigma$, and $\beta_1(t_i) = 0 = t_i \bmod J$. ✓

*Inductive step:* Assume $\beta_n$ satisfies (a), (b). The surjection $R[t]/J^{n+1} \to R[t]/J^n$ has kernel $J^n/J^{n+1}$, which is **square-zero** (since $J^{2n} \subset J^{n+1}$ for $n \geq 1$). By formal smoothness, $\beta_n$ admits a lift $\tilde{\beta}_{n+1}: S \to R[t]/J^{n+1}$.

Any two lifts differ by an $R$-derivation $\delta: S \to J^n/J^{n+1}$ (standard fact: if two ring maps agree mod a square-zero ideal, their difference is a derivation). We need $\beta_{n+1}(t_i) = t_i \bmod J^{n+1}$, i.e., $\delta(t_i) = t_i - \tilde{\beta}_{n+1}(t_i) \bmod J^{n+1}$. Set $c_i := t_i - \tilde{\beta}_{n+1}(t_i) \in J^n/J^{n+1}$ (this lies in $J^n/J^{n+1}$ because $\tilde{\beta}_{n+1}(t_i) \equiv \beta_n(t_i) \equiv t_i \bmod J^n$).

By the key consequence above, since $J^n/J^{n+1}$ is an $R$-module (via $\beta_n$) and $I/I^2$ is free, there exists a unique $R$-derivation $\delta: S \to J^n/J^{n+1}$ with $\delta(t_i) = c_i$. Setting $\beta_{n+1} = \tilde{\beta}_{n+1} + \delta$ gives the desired lift satisfying (b). ✓

The compatible system $\{\beta_n\}$ yields a continuous $R$-algebra map $\beta: S \to R[[t_1, \dots, t_d]]$ with $\beta(t_i) = t_i$ and $\beta|_R = \mathrm{id}$. Since $\beta(I) \subset J$, this extends to $\beta^\wedge: S^\wedge \to R[[t_1, \dots, t_d]]$.

---

**$\beta^\wedge \circ \alpha^\wedge = \mathrm{id}$ on $R[[t_1, \dots, t_d]]$.** The composition $\beta \circ \alpha: R[t_1, \dots, t_d] \to R[[t_1, \dots, t_d]]$ satisfies $(\beta \circ \alpha)(r) = r$ and $(\beta \circ \alpha)(t_i) = t_i$. Hence $\beta \circ \alpha$ is the natural inclusion $R[t] \hookrightarrow R[[t]]$, and on completions $\beta^\wedge \circ \alpha^\wedge = \mathrm{id}$. ✓

**$\alpha^\wedge \circ \beta^\wedge = \mathrm{id}$ on $S^\wedge$.** Let $\iota: S \to S^\wedge$ be the natural map, and set $\gamma := \alpha^\wedge \circ \beta: S \to S^\wedge$. Both $\gamma$ and $\iota$ are $R$-algebra maps with $\gamma(t_i) = t_i$ and $\gamma|_R = \mathrm{id}$. We show $\gamma \equiv \iota \pmod{I^n}$ for all $n$ by induction.

*Base case $n=1$:* Both reduce to $\sigma: S \to S/I = R$ modulo $I$. ✓

*Inductive step:* Assume $\gamma \equiv \iota \pmod{I^n}$. View $\gamma, \iota$ as maps $S \to S/I^{n+1}$. They agree mod $I^n$, and $I^n/I^{n+1}$ is square-zero in $S/I^{n+1}$, so $\delta := \gamma - \iota: S \to I^n/I^{n+1}$ is an $R$-derivation. Since $I$ acts trivially on $I^n/I^{n+1}$, this derivation corresponds to an $R$-linear map $I/I^2 \to I^n/I^{n+1}$. But $\delta(t_i) = \gamma(t_i) - \iota(t_i) = 0$ for all $i$, and $\bar{t}_1, \dots, \bar{t}_d$ form a basis of $I/I^2$, so this $R$-linear map is zero. Hence $\delta = 0$, i.e., $\gamma \equiv \iota \pmod{I^{n+1}}$. ✓

By induction, $\gamma = \iota$ in $S^\wedge$, so $\alpha^\wedge \circ \beta^\wedge = \mathrm{id}$ on $S^\wedge$. ✓

---

**Conclusion.** The maps $\alpha^\wedge: R[[t_1, \dots, t_d]] \to S^\wedge$ and $\beta^\wedge: S^\wedge \to R[[t_1, \dots, t_d]]$ are mutually inverse $R$-algebra isomorphisms. Therefore
$$S^\wedge \cong R[[t_1, \dots, t_d]]$$
as $R$-algebras, where $d = \mathrm{rank}_R(I/I^2)$. $\blacksquare$

Since $I/I^2$ is a free $R$-module (of rank $d$, say), choose $t_1, \dots, t_d \in I$ whose images $\bar{t}_1, \dots, \bar{t}_d$ form an $R$-basis of $I/I^2$.

**Conormal sequence.** For the sequence of maps $R \xrightarrow{\varphi} S \to S/I = R$, the conormal exact sequence reads
$$I/I^2 \longrightarrow \Omega_{S/R} \otimes_S R \longrightarrow \Omega_{R/R} \longrightarrow 0.$$
Since $\Omega_{R/R} = 0$ (the map $R \to S/I = R$ is the identity), we get a surjection $I/I^2 \twoheadrightarrow \Omega_{S/R} \otimes_S R$. Because $\varphi$ is **smooth**, this sequence is also left-exact (a standard property of smooth maps: the conormal sequence $0 \to I/I^2 \to \Omega_{S/R}\otimes S/I \to \Omega_{(S/I)/R} \to 0$ is short exact). $$I/I^2 \cong \Omega_{S/R} \otimes_S R.$$
In particular, $dt_1, \dots, dt_d$ form a basis of $\Omega_{S/R} \otimes_S R$.

**Key consequence for derivations.** For any $R$-module $M$ (viewed as an $S$-module via $S \to S/I = R$), $R$-derivations $\delta: S \to M$ correspond to $S$-linear maps $\Omega_{S/R} \to M$, which (since $I$ acts trivially on $M$) correspond to $R$-linear maps $\Omega_{S/R} \otimes_S R \to M$, i.e., to $R$-linear maps $I/I^2 \to M$.
